Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.30 5 Homomorphisms, isomorphisms and quotient groups 5.1 Quotient groups Suppose H ≤ G. We want to be able to create a group by “dividing” G by H to form the set G/H of cosets of H in G. Can we do this? No! The set G/H is not always a group. However, when H is normal in G this does work, and is called a quotient group. Definition 5.1.1. Suppose N ⊴ G. The quotient group G/N is the set of cosets of N in G with the following operation: for all cosets aN ∈ G/N and all bN ∈ G/N , aN ∗ bN = (ab)N. [Note that in fact (aN)(bN) = abN even without this definition, since (aN )(bN ) = a(N b)N = a(bN )N (by normality) = abN .] We must prove that this is indeed a group by checking the axioms. Proof: We must check that the following axioms hold: closure; identity; inverses; associativity. Choose any three cosets aN, bN, cN ∈ G/N . • Closure: Now aN ∗ bN = (ab)N , and (ab)N is a coset of N in G so it lies in G/N . • Identity: Define e to be eGN = N . We will show that this definition of e satisfies the properties of the identity for G/N . First note that e ∗ (aN ) = eGN ∗ aN = (eGa)N = aN and (aN ) ∗ e = (aN )(eGN ) = (aeG)N = aN . • Inverses: Now a −1N is a coset of N in G, and so it lies in G/N . Furthermore, (a−1N ) ∗ (aN ) = (a −1a)N = N = e. Also (aN ) ∗ (a−1N ) = (aa −1)N = N = e. Therefore a −1N is the inverse of aN . • Associativity: (aN ) ∗ ((bN ) ∗ (cN )) = (aN ) ∗ ((bc)N ) = (a(bc))N = ((ab)c)N = (ab)N ∗ cN = (aN ∗ bN ) ∗ cN . Example 5.1.2. You probably saw this example in Algebraic Strcutures. Consider the group (Z, +). It is abelian, so every subgroup is a normal subgroup. We know that 3Z is a subgroup, therefore it is a normal subgroup and hence (Z, +)/3Z is a group. What does (Z, +)/3Z look like? Well, (Z, +)/3Z = {0 + 3Z, 1 + 3Z, 2 + 3Z} (because 3 + 3Z = 3Z, 4 + 3Z = 1 + 3Z, etc) Hence (Z, +)/3Z and Z3 have the same elements. Moreover, their group operations are the same: both operations are addition mod 3. Hence (Z, +)/3Z = Z3. Example 5.1.3. Recall that S3 = {e, (123), (132), (12), (13), (23)} and C3 = {e, (123), (132)}. One can show that C3 ⊴ S3 (this is a question on one of your problem sheets). Therefore S3/C3 is a group. What does S3/C3 look like? Well, it has order [S3 ∶ C3] = ∣S3∣/∣C3∣ = 6/3 = 2. There are just two cosets of C3 in S3 (and one of these cosets is just C3 itself). Therefore any element not in C3 will give us the other coset. E.g. S3 = C3 ∪ (12)C3. Hence the quotient group is S3/C3 = {eC3, (12)C3}. The operation is: (eC3)(eC3) = (ee)C3 = eC3 (eC3)((12)C3) = (e(12))C3 = (12)C3 ((12)C3)(eC3) = ((12)e)C3 = (12)C3 ((12)C3)((12)C3) = ((12)(12))C3 = eC3 As you can see, the group S3/C3 is behaving exactly like the group {e, (12)} = C2 — the only difference is in the symbols used for the group elements. This is an example of an isomorphism, that we will cover in the next section.

Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.31 5.2 Homomorphisms Definition 5.2.1. Let G be a group with operation ∗ and let H be a group with operation #. A function θ ∶ G → H that satisfies θ(g1 ∗ g2) = θ(g1)#θ(g2) for all g1, g2 ∈ G is called a homomorphism. (Notice that θ(g1) and θ(g2) are in H which is why the operation becomes #.) However, because we are now doing grown-up Group Theory, we don’t bother writing in the symbols ∗ and #, and instead say that a homomorphism is a map θ ∶ G → H that satisfies θ(g1g2) = θ(g1)θ(g2). The reader is expected to remember that the group operation between g1 and g2 will not necessarily be the same as the group operation between θ(g1) and θ(g2). The kernel of θ is denoted Ker(θ) and is the set of all elements in G that are mapped to eH . The image of θ is denoted Im(θ) (or sometimes θ(G)) and is the set of all images of elements in G. More precisely: Ker(θ) = {g ∈ G ∶ θ(g) = eH} and Im(θ) = {θ(g) ∶ g ∈ G}. Example 5.2.2. Here is a homomorphism. • Let n ∈ N. The map φ ∶ Z → Zn given by φ(m) = [m]n for all m ∈ Z is a homomorphism. Proof: Fix m1, m2 ∈ Z. On one hand, φ(m1 + m2) = [m1 + m2]n. On the other hand, φ(m1) ⊕ φ(m2) = [m1]n ⊕ [m2]n and by the definition of Zn we know [m1]n ⊕ [m2]n = [m1 + m2]n. Hence φ(m1 + m2) = φ(m1) ⊕ φ(m2) for all m1, m2 ∈ Z so φ is a homomorphism. • Ker(φ) = {m ∈ Z ∶ [m]n = [0]n} = nZ = the set of multiples of n. Note that φ is not one-to-one because more than one element in Z is mapped to [0]n ∈ Zn. • Im(φ) = {φ(m) ∶ m ∈ Z} = {[0]n, [1]n, . . . , [n − 1]n}. Since Im(φ) = Zn, we see that φ is onto. Non-Example 5.2.3. Here is an example of a map π from S3 to C3 that is not a homomorphism: • π(e) = e • π((1 2 3)) = (1 2 3) and π((1 3 2)) = (1 3 2) • π(σ) = e for all 2-cycles σ The map π fails to be a homomorphism because (1 3)(1 2) = (1 2 3) but • π((1 3))π((1 2)) = ee = e • π((1 2 3)) = (1 2 3) Hence π((1 3))π((1 2)) /= π((1 3)(1 2)), so π cannot be a homomorphism. Proposition 5.2.4. Let G and H be groups with θ ∶ G → H a homomorphism. Then: (i) θ(eG) = eH (ii) θ(gm) = (θ(g)) m for all g ∈ G and all m ∈ Z (iii) Im(θ) ≤ H [Note: in general Im(θ) ⋬ H] (iv) Ker(θ) ⊴ G Proof. You will prove each of these things on a problem sheet. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism between two groups. If there is an isomorphism between groups G and H, they are essentially the same group, and we write G ≅ H. We will explore isomorphisms in detail in the next subsection.
